exams.key: 14. Gases, Wate and Solutions Test - Marking Key.docx
Test 5 - Acid Base Precipitation Gases answers.docx

notes: The given +1 ion configuration has 26 electrons, whereas the supplied rubidium answer requires 36 electrons (2,8,18,8). Review the printed configuration.
Supplied key D conflicts with the liquid-mercury wording: liquid malleability (A) is also problematic. Review the stem and intended answer.
Supplied key selects A (3), which counts lone pairs on one chlorine atom. Cl₂ has 6 lone pairs in total, giving B. Automatic marking is disabled.
The list includes volume as a factor changing volume, apparently in place of temperature. Supplied key D is preserved; review the wording.
Supplied key C does not reflect ionisation of HCl in water. Option D describes covalent bonds broken and covalent/ion–dipole interactions formed. Teacher review is required.
Paper and guide use different energy-profile levels; read the values from the paper graph before marking.
Matching marking guide labels this question 9; paper labels it 8.
Paper header allocates 5 marks, but the calculation subpart prints 6 marks. Header allocation retained.
The guide’s methylbenzene side-chain chlorination requires UV light, which is not specified in the paper. Review reaction conditions.
The supplied 90 ppm answer conflicts with the plotted calibration line: peak area 12,000 corresponds to approximately 125–130 ppm. Review before marking.
Citric acid is triprotic; the paper describes it as monoprotic. Review this model simplification before use.
The stated −210°C is near nitrogen’s freezing point; ordinary liquid-nitrogen bath temperature is approximately −196°C. Review the supplied temperature.

sourceNotes: Reaction Rates paper contains 3 written questions despite its cover listing 4; guide question 9 matches paper question 8.
Gases Water and Solutions individual allocations total 60 marks; cover says 61.
IMF Solutions written questions total 45 marks; written-section heading says 50, while the cover correctly totals 55.
